title: cfDNA Release Following Carotid Revascularization: Comparison of Carotid Endarterectomy and Carotid Artery Stenting in Internal Carotid Artery Stenosis
summary:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is released during cellular injury and can be detected in the bloodstream as a marker of tissue stress and inflammatory processes. This study investigates whether cfDNA release differs between two established treatment strategies for severe carotid artery stenosis: carotid endarterectomy (CEA) and minimally invasive carotid artery stenting (CAS).
Particular focus is placed on potential subclinical neurological injury that may occur during the intervention due to transient cerebral hypoperfusion or microembolic events. To address this, cfDNA concentrations will be measured before and after the procedure and correlated with neurological assessments, established biomarkers of neuronal injury, as well as parameters of cerebral oxygenation and autoregulation.
In addition, methylation analyses will be performed to determine whether specific cfDNA fractions originate from neuronal tissue. This approach may help to detect subtle cerebral injury or blood–brain barrier disruption at an early stage.
In the long term, the study aims to establish cfDNA as a minimally invasive biomarker for risk stratification and peri-interventional monitoring in patients undergoing vascular interventions.
conditions: Occlusion and stenosis of carotid artery

interventions.name:
Patients undergoing Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
• Potentially increased risk of microembolic events and subsequent neuronal injury.
• Pre- and postoperative cfDNA assessment in combination with neurological outcome evaluation.

Patients undergoing Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS)
• Comparison of cfDNA release and neurological outcome under different patterns of mechanical vascular stress.
• cfDNA assessment and neurological outcome evaluation likewise performed.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Age ≥ 18 years
• Written informed consent for study participation
• Planned carotid endarterectomy (CEA) or carotid artery stenting (CAS) for high-grade asymptomatic internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis of 70–90% according to NASCET criteria
• No pre-existing neurological deficits (mRS > 2)
• Ability to participate in follow-up assessments
• Stenosis amenable to treatment with both CEA and CAS (no anatomical preference)
Exclusion criteria:
• Incomplete performance of the planned surgical intervention (e.g., aborted CEA or CAS procedure)
